terms.definition: The ordered sequence a cell passes through in order to divide into two: a long preparatory period called interphase, made up of G1, S phase and G2, followed by a short M phase in which the chromosomes are sorted and the cell is cut in two. The word cycle suggests a fixed circuit run at a fixed speed, and that part of the everyday sense misleads. Progress between phases is driven by cyclin-dependent kinase activity and is conditional on specific physical states being satisfied, so the same cycle can take very different times in two cells of the same type.

The part of the cell cycle outside M phase, comprising G1, S phase and G2. A cell in interphase is not resting: it grows, makes protein, and in S phase replicates its DNA. In an illustrative cultured human cycle of about 24 hours, interphase occupies roughly 95 per cent of the time, which is why a snapshot of any tissue shows very few cells caught in the act of dividing.

A surveillance mechanism that makes a later step of the cell cycle conditional on an earlier step having been completed correctly. It detects a specific physical state and holds a transition while that state is unsatisfactory. Three features are easy to get wrong. It contains no clock, so it can pass a cell in minutes or hold it for hours depending only on what it detects. It is not a place in the cycle. And it is not absolute: a checkpoint delays rather than permanently blocks, and it can be satisfied by a wrong state that happens to look like the state it tests for.

A protein whose concentration rises and falls through the cell cycle and which must be bound to a cyclin-dependent kinase for that kinase to have any activity. Different cyclins partner different kinases at different points, so which cyclins are currently present is in effect a record of which phase the cell is in. Cyclin D and cyclin E act with their partner kinases in G1; cyclin B partners the kinase that maintains the mitotic state, and its slow destruction during a prolonged mitotic arrest is what eventually lets an arrested cell escape.

An enzyme that drives cell-cycle transitions by adding phosphate to target proteins, and which has no kinase activity at all unless it is tightly bound to a cyclin. This makes it a switch with two independent off positions: remove its cyclin, or leave the cyclin in place and add an inhibitor protein that rearranges the active site. Checkpoints use both routes. A cyclin-dependent kinase is the actuator that moves the cycle forward, which is a different job from the surveillance that decides whether it may fire.

A transition in G1 beyond which a cell no longer requires external growth-factor signalling and will complete the cycle on its own. Treat it as a real change of state whose position is fuzzy rather than as a line ruled across G1: published estimates of when cells cross it vary widely even within a single cell type, and whether one such universal point exists in G1 has been questioned in the literature.

A reversible state in which a cell is not cycling but can be brought back into the cycle, commonly labelled G0. The evidence is that it is a separate biological state and not simply a long G1, and that it is not one state but a heterogeneous collection of related conditions; distinguishing a quiescent cell from a cell in early G1 is difficult in practice. Most crypt stem cells are not dividing at any given moment, which is consistent with PREM-BIO-001's point that a stem cell is defined by capacity rather than by continuous activity.

One linear DNA molecule together with the proteins packaged with it. This lesson uses only the minimum needed to explain segregation: that the genome is divided among more than twenty such molecules, that each carries one centromere, and that S phase leaves each one as two attached copies. How chromatin is organised, how many copies of each chromosome a cell carries, and what a locus is belong to a separate outcome, PREM-06.02 Chromosomes and genomes, which has no lesson yet and which this lesson defers to rather than anticipating.

One of the two identical copies of a chromosome produced when S phase replicates it, while the two remain physically attached to each other. Because they are identical, it does not matter which daughter cell receives which; what matters is that each daughter receives exactly one. They are held together by cohesin from S phase until anaphase, and the cutting of that link is the step that commits a cell to finishing its division.

The specialised region of a chromosome at which the machinery of segregation grips it. It is where the kinetochore is assembled, and therefore where the spindle's pulling force is applied. One centromere per chromosome means one gripping point per chromosome, which is why an error at a single centromere can affect the whole division.

The protein structure assembled on a centromere, to which spindle microtubules attach and which reports its own attachment state to the spindle assembly checkpoint. Each of the two sister chromatids carries one. A kinetochore that is not properly engaged assembles the complex that blocks anaphase, and a single such kinetochore is enough to hold an entire cell. Exactly which physical variable a kinetochore reports, whether microtubule occupancy or mechanical tension, is unresolved.

The microtubule apparatus built at mitosis that attaches to kinetochores and pulls the sister chromatids to opposite poles. It does a second job that is easy to miss: the position of the anaphase spindle also determines where the cleavage furrow forms, so the structure that sorts the chromosomes is the structure that locates the cut. A cell therefore never has to work out where its own middle is.

The sorting of duplicated chromosomes into two complete sets, conventionally divided into prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. Each transition is better read as a condition than as a scene change: condensed chromosomes appear, microtubules attach to kinetochores, and anaphase begins when the link between sister chromatids is broken. Mitosis is the sorting; cutting the cell in two is cytokinesis, a separate operation with its own machinery and its own checkpoint.

A ring-shaped protein complex that holds sister chromatids together from S phase until the metaphase-to-anaphase transition. Anaphase happens when the ring is opened by cleavage of its RAD21 subunit. Because that cut cannot be reversed, cohesin is the reason a cell's checking has to happen before anaphase rather than during it.

The enzyme that cleaves cohesin's RAD21 subunit, opening the ring and allowing sister chromatids to separate. It is held inactive until the metaphase-to-anaphase transition by an inhibitory chaperone, securin. Its action is the irreversible step of a division, which is why it is kept behind two locks rather than one.

An inhibitory chaperone that keeps separase inactive until the metaphase-to-anaphase transition. It is destroyed by ubiquitination by the APC/C, and its destruction is the last controllable step before cohesin is cut. A checkpoint that wants to stop a division has to act at or before this point.

The ubiquitin ligase that marks securin for destruction, thereby releasing separase and triggering anaphase. It is the target of the spindle assembly checkpoint: while the checkpoint is on, this complex is blocked, so securin survives and the chromatids stay joined. Written APC/C throughout this lesson to keep it apart from the unrelated protein abbreviated APC in PREM-BIO-006.

alignment.note: PREM-BIO-006 defines APC as adenomatous polyposis coli, the scaffold of the beta-catenin destruction complex. This lesson's APC/C is an unrelated assembly with a different job; the two share only an abbreviation, and nothing in lesson six's definition is altered. The literature resolves the collision by writing this one APC/C, which this lesson does throughout, and the learner is given the disambiguation in prose where the term first appears: Wnt and colorectal adenomas mean lesson six's protein, anaphase and ubiquitin mean this one.

terms.definition: The surveillance mechanism that keeps APC/C inactive until the chromosomes are properly attached to the spindle, working through a complex assembled at kinetochores that are not correctly engaged. A single unattached kinetochore is sufficient to sustain the arrest. Two limits matter as much as the mechanism: it is satisfied by a merotelic attachment, which is wrong but presents neither an unattached kinetochore nor an absence of tension, and it gives way after several hours as cyclin B decays.

The tetrameric complex of MAD2, CDC20, BUBR1 and BUB3 that assembles in response to kinetochores that are not correctly attached, and that binds APC/C-CDC20 to block its activity. It is the physical form the spindle assembly checkpoint's signal takes, and it is what a single unattached kinetochore is enough to keep supplied.

The correct kinetochore-microtubule configuration, in which the two sister kinetochores are attached to microtubules coming from opposite spindle poles. It produces tension across the sister kinetochores and leaves no kinetochore unattached, which is why the spindle assembly checkpoint permits anaphase. The awkward fact this lesson is built on is that a merotelic attachment produces both of those same conditions while being wrong.

A configuration in which a single kinetochore is connected to microtubules from both spindle poles at once. It does not trigger a checkpoint-dependent delay of anaphase, because like a correct attachment it generates tension across the sister kinetochores and leaves no kinetochore unattached. The chromatid is then pulled toward both poles and lags at anaphase. Merotely is the clean demonstration that a wrong state can satisfy a working checkpoint; it is not established as the main cause of aneuploidy, and that question is disputed.

A chromatid left behind near the spindle midzone during anaphase instead of travelling cleanly to a pole, characteristically the consequence of a merotelic attachment pulling it in two directions. A laggard that persists there to the end of division is packaged into a micronucleus. Note that lagging and missegregating are different events: a laggard can end up in the correct daughter cell.

A small separate nucleus formed around a chromatid that was left near the spindle midzone at the end of division, rather than being included in either daughter's main nucleus. It is the visible record that a division went mechanically wrong. What becomes of a cell carrying one is the subject of PREM-BIO-010 of this block, not of this lesson.

The escape of a cell from a spindle-checkpoint arrest without having divided, leaving one cell containing both sets of chromosomes. It happens because cyclin B is slowly destroyed throughout the arrest even while the checkpoint remains demonstrably active, until too little remains to sustain the mitotic state. In human retinal pigment epithelial cells the arrest lasted on the order of nine to fifteen hours before slippage. This is why a checkpoint should be understood as a delay with a limit rather than as a gate.

The asynchronous separation of sister chromatids caused by the spindle's own pulling forces during a prolonged metaphase delay, occurring without separase and with cohesin still present on the separated chromatids. It appeared after a few hours of induced delay in the systems where it was measured. Its significance for this lesson is that waiting, which is the only remedy a checkpoint has, is itself a source of error once it goes on long enough.

The physical division of one cell into two after its chromosomes have been sorted, carried out by a contractile ring that constricts the cell at its equator and completed by abscission of the membrane bridge that remains. It is a separate operation from mitosis, with its own machinery and its own checkpoint, and it can fail on its own: a cell whose cytokinesis fails is left with two nuclei and twice the normal DNA content, and no checkpoint stops it dividing again.

The ring of filamentous actin and myosin II that assembles beneath the plasma membrane at the cell's equator and constricts to draw the membrane inward as a cleavage furrow. Its components are the ones PREM-BIO-007 of this block introduced for microvilli and junctions, put to a third use. Where it assembles is set by the anaphase spindle, through a signalling chain that ends in a zone of active RhoA at the equatorial cortex.

The final severing of the membrane bridge that still joins two daughter cells after the contractile ring has constricted, carried out by the ESCRT-III machinery at the midbody. In cultured human cells it follows anaphase by about an hour and a half. It has its own checkpoint: when chromatin is caught in the bridge, abscission is delayed, which avoids both breaking the DNA and fusing the daughters back into one cell.

The part of a renewing tissue whose cells are currently dividing. In a human colonic crypt it occupies the bottom third of the tube and accounts for about a quarter of the crypt's cells, identified by staining for the proliferation antigen Ki-67. It contains a small number of stem cells and a much larger number of transit-amplifying cells, and its size relative to the whole crypt is the quantity from which this lesson derives the tissue's cycle time.

The share of a tissue's cells that are dividing, obtained by dividing the number of proliferating cells by the total. For the human colonic crypt counted by Ki-67 staining it is about 0.257. It is more useful than either count on its own, because published totals for a crypt disagree while the ratio is what determines the compartment's cycle time: multiply the proliferative fraction by the tissue's turnover time and the crypt's size cancels out.

A dividing cell descended from a stem cell that undergoes a limited number of further divisions before it stops and differentiates. Amplifying cells are most of a crypt's proliferative compartment and supply nearly all of its output, because the handful of stem cells at the base divide too slowly to do so themselves. They also cycle faster than those stem cells, which inverts the natural assumption that the stem cell is the busiest cell in the tissue.

A cell with the capacity to self-renew and to produce differentiated progeny. Capacity is not continuous activity: a human colonic crypt holds between 5 and 10 active stem cells that each divide only about once every two to three days, so most are not dividing at any given moment. They are the slowest-dividing cells in the dividing part of the crypt, and the speed of renewal lives in their amplifying daughters.

alignment.note: PREM-BIO-001 defined a stem cell by its capacity to self-renew and produce differentiated progeny, and was explicit that capacity is not continuous activity; PREM-BIO-006 adopted that meaning unchanged and deferred what division involves to this lesson. This lesson keeps the same meaning and nothing is narrowed or extended. What it adds is the division arithmetic lesson one deferred: how many stem cells a crypt holds, how often each divides, and why that rate makes an amplifying compartment arithmetically necessary.

terms.definition: The stochastic replacement of stem cells in which no lineage has an advantage, so that a lineage's descendants expand or vanish by chance, following a one-dimensional random walk. In human colonic crypts it means that all but one stem lineage eventually disappears and the crypt becomes the descendant of a single stem cell, with a median time of about 6.3 years. It is why a mutation in one crypt stem cell has a chance of taking over the crypt without needing to confer any benefit.

A chromosome content that departs from the normal complement, as arises when a division gives one daughter too many copies of a chromosome and the other too few. It is the persistent consequence of a segregation error: a cell cannot repair it the way it repairs a broken strand of DNA. Measured missegregation rates in cultured near-diploid human cells are about 0.025 per cent per chromosome per division; no rate has been established for cells in a human colonic crypt.

Carrying twice the normal complement of chromosomes, as a cell does when it exits mitosis without dividing or when its cytokinesis fails. Two routes in this lesson produce it: mitotic slippage out of a checkpoint arrest, and outright failure of the cleavage. Neither is caught by any checkpoint, and binucleate primary human cells produced by cleavage failure went on to replicate their DNA and re-enter mitosis at close to normal frequency.
